edges.label: The 'outside of government so the technology could remain proprietary' formulation is what the eminent domain provision was written to defeat
edges.note: Section 9010 asserts federal eminent domain over recovered technologies 'controlled by private persons or entities.' Reasoning: the legislative remedy matches the mechanism AARO records interviewees describing; no drafting record ties the two documents.

edges.label: Proposal versus enactment
edges.note: Division I of the Senate-passed H.R. 2670 contained a Review Board and eminent domain; P.L. 118-31 as enacted did not. The gap between these two documents is the domain boundary.

edges.label: reduced to secs. 1841-1843 in conference
edges.note: Public Law 118-31 contains no eminent domain clause, no Review Board and no contractor inspection authority. Congress asserted jurisdiction over the paper and left the objects where they are.

a.label: UAP Disclosure Act of 2023 (S.Amdt. 797 to S. 2226; Division G of the Senate-passed FY2024 NDAA)

edges.label: The Senate voted to seize privately held recovered technology by eminent domain
edges.note: The Senate passed Division I of the NDAA on 27 July 2023 including Sec. 9010, and defined 'legacy program' to include 'commercial industry... and private sector endeavors to collect, exploit, or reverse engineer technologies of unknown origin.' No named company is in the text; the provision only has meaning if some entity holds something.
